variant.text: Task data originates from MIMIC-IV v2.2, a PhysioNet snapshot from January 2023. Each task record preserves the source patient identifier, enabling complete traceability from any task back to its underlying patient record.

All patient records originate from a de-identified hospital database collected during routine care between 2008 and 2019. The data are released under a credentialed-access data use agreement, and the source institution's review board determined that the study qualified for a waiver of consent.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.
Contamination mitigation includes gating access to the test split. Measurement of verbatim overlap with public web corpora revealed zero exact matches between test tasks and public sources.

The agent cannot reach ground-truth answers at run time: the answer labels are stored in a separate evaluation service that has no network path from the agent sandbox, and they are not published in the repository.

The environment is frozen at release: the database snapshot, the software image and the simulated-patient language model are all pinned to fixed versions, and no external service is called at evaluation time other than the model under test.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
A random-action agent succeeds on 3.1% of tasks, and the chance success rate for each metric is reported in the appendix.
We also report a baseline in which the same language model answers without access to any tools.
The evaluator uses a language model to compare each answer with the reference.
All runs use temperature 0 and a fixed random seed, and each task is run three times; this repeated-run policy is described in the main text.
We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all model scores and test the difference between the two best models with a paired permutation test (p = 0.02).
Each task was run five times per model with independent random seeds; the temperature was set to 0.7, and the reported scores are means over the five independent runs.

We report 95% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping over tasks, so the resampling unit is the task; where several tasks share a patient, we resample patients instead to account for clustering.

Models were queried through their APIs using the snapshot identifiers gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, with temperature 0 and a maximum of 2,048 output tokens; all reported numbers correspond to harness release v1.2.0.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.

The write actions that change patient state (medication orders, notes and messages) are listed in a table. Writes are executed against a sandboxed copy of the record, and unnecessary or unsafe writes are penalised in the score. The agent prompt states that writes are sandboxed.
Grading operates on the final environment state. Grader validation tested 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, yielding 1% false acceptance and 2% false rejection rates.

Agents have no web access during runs and retrieval tools are restricted to the task environment, so answers cannot leak through external search. A private held-out split with hidden labels is kept off all public surfaces, and every released task carries a canary string.
We report accuracy per task family (diagnosis, ordering and documentation tasks) and per patient subgroup by sex and race, and each table lists the number of cases in every slice.

The patient records are real de-identified records from a hospital database. Their use was approved under a data use agreement requiring credentialed access and de-identification by the safe harbour method, and the data are released under terms separate from the MIT code licence.
